prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Mary who mattered to me, gone or asleep among fruits, spilled in ash, in dust, I did not leave you. Even now I can't keep from composing you, limbs & blue cloak & soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name, I say there is no Mary except the word Mary, no trace on the dust of my pillowslip. I only dream of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees above you murmuring into a crown. Antique queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you, here the heavy-winged doves, asleep by the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed carefully in the syllables of your name, in the air and the sea of them, the sharp scent of their sea foam. What is the matter with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I look behind? I carried you a long way into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out. Mary, I am still for you, I am still a numbness for you.

The speaker mourns Mary’s absence by reconstructing her through lyrical repetition, dreams, and sensuous images of fruit, flowers, birds, and the sea. Yet Mary survives only as a name and imagined presence, revealing both language’s power to preserve love and its inability to overcome loss.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Mary, Even, Antique

outputs.L1:
Mary, who mattered to me, gone or asleep among fruits, spilled into ash, into dust—I did not leave you. Even now, I cannot keep from composing you: limbs and blue cloak and soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name. I say there is no Mary except the word *Mary*, no trace upon the dust of my pillow slip. I dream only of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees above you, murmuring themselves into a crown.

Antique queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you; here, the heavy-winged doves asleep beside the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed carefully in the syllables of your name—in the air and sea of them, in the sharp scent of their sea foam.

What is the matter with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I look behind? I carried you a long way into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out. Mary, I am still for you. I am still a numbness for you.
outputs.L2: Mary, beloved by me, whether dead or merely sleeping amid fruit, scattered into cinders and earth, I never abandoned you. Still, I cannot stop remaking your image: your body, pale-blue mantle, and gentle hands. I fall asleep hearing your name and insist that Mary exists nowhere beyond the name itself, leaving no mark in the powdery fabric of my pillow. I dream only of shadowed violets grazing your ankles and bees humming over you like a wreath. Ancient sovereign, while darkness continues dreaming, I offer you pears rinsed clean and broad-winged pigeons resting beside the hyacinths. I stand here after immersing myself in every sound of your name—in its atmosphere, its ocean, and the biting fragrance of its surf. What has happened to me? Mary, behind which word or layer of dust could I possibly find you? I bore you deep into my reflection, trusting that you would lead me out again. Mary, I remain devoted to you; for you, I remain without feeling.
outputs.L3:
The speaker mourns Mary’s absence while firmly insisting that they have never abandoned her memory. Although Mary is physically gone, she remains a constant presence in the speaker’s inner life. She survives most powerfully through her name, which the speaker repeats, dreams of, and transforms into poetry. Language becomes both an act of devotion and an attempt to keep her from disappearing completely.

Mary’s remembered image is elevated through vivid natural imagery. Fruit, flowers, bees, doves, and sea foam surround her with beauty, fertility, purity, and mystery, making her appear less like an ordinary person than an almost mythical queen. Yet this idealization does not ease the speaker’s pain. Instead, the speaker questions the nature of their grief and searches helplessly for some remaining trace of Mary behind words, memories, and dust.

Ultimately, the speaker remains emotionally numb but unwaveringly devoted. They had hoped that preserving Mary’s name and image in poetry would also bring personal healing. However, the act of remembrance offers no clear release: it keeps Mary present, but it cannot restore her or fully console the person who mourns her.
outputs.L4:
Mary’s absence shapes the speaker’s entire experience of the world. Unable to recover her physically, the speaker attempts to recreate her through language, repeatedly invoking her name as though repetition might summon her back. Dreams provide another temporary refuge: in imagination, the separation between past and present, presence and absence, can briefly dissolve. Yet these visions never become fully real. Each act of remembrance therefore offers both consolation and renewed pain, since imagining Mary only emphasizes that she is no longer there.

The poem’s sensuous natural imagery deepens this attempt at reconstruction. Fruit, flowers, birds, and the sea evoke color, fragrance, sound, movement, and touch, giving Mary’s remembered presence an almost physical intensity. These images suggest beauty, abundance, and vitality, but they also carry associations with ripeness, transience, migration, and change. Flowers fade, fruit decays, birds depart, and the sea remains restless and unreachable. The natural world thus reflects the speaker’s grief: it seems to preserve traces of Mary everywhere, while continually reminding the speaker that nothing beautiful can be permanently possessed.

Lyrical repetition is central to this tension. Mary’s name functions like a refrain, prayer, or incantation. By speaking it again and again, the speaker protects her from complete disappearance and turns private mourning into poetic form. At the same time, the repetition exposes the limits of that effort. A name can evoke memories and emotions, but it cannot restore the person to whom it refers. The more insistently Mary is addressed, the more clearly her silence is felt.

Mary consequently survives within the poem as an imagined presence suspended between memory and desire. Language gives her shape, surrounds her with beauty, and allows love to endure beyond separation. Nevertheless, the poem does not pretend that art can conquer death or absence. Its power lies instead in preserving the trace of what has been lost. Through dreams, repetition, and sensuous imagery, the speaker keeps Mary emotionally alive, even while acknowledging that poetry can memorialize love but cannot return its beloved object.
outputs.L5:
Mary stepped into the antique shop just as the evening light faded. Dust shimmered above shelves crowded with clocks, silver mirrors, and faded books. Even the quietest objects seemed to whisper their histories.

At the back of the shop, Mary discovered a small wooden music box. Its delicate melody felt strangely familiar, like a song from a forgotten dream. Beneath it, she found an inscription: *For Mary, until we meet again.*

The antique had been waiting for her.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem addressed to a lost woman named Mary, blending grief, longing, dreams, fruit, flowers, bees, doves, dust, and the sea.
counterfactuals.output:
Mary, the rooms have forgotten your footsteps, but not the light that followed them. It lingers on the table where peaches soften into gold, where figs split open like small, sweet wounds, where a glass of water keeps the pale memory of your mouth.

At night I dream you are walking through an orchard in bloom. Bees stitch their low music through the branches, and every flower turns toward you as if you were the sun returning. I call your name, but doves rise from the grass in a white astonishment, scattering my voice among their wings.

Mary, I have carried grief until it became a country: its roads are dust, its houses empty, its fields blue with flowers no one planted. Sometimes I find your shadow there, kneeling beside the wild roses, gathering fallen pears into your dress. Sometimes you look up. Sometimes you almost speak.

But morning comes with its dry hands. It touches everything to dust—the bed, the mirror, the letters folded beneath my heart. Only longing refuses to fade. It ripens in me, dark and fragrant, a fruit I cannot swallow or set down.

Beyond the window, the sea keeps breathing. It draws the world toward itself and gives nothing back but salt, shells, and broken light. I think you are somewhere beyond it, Mary, asleep beneath a sky of endless flowers, while bees dream in their hives and doves settle softly along the shore.

If you hear me, come near—not as a ghost, not as sorrow, but as rain upon the dust. Come as the scent of orange blossoms at dusk, as a red plum opening in the hand, as one white feather turning in the wind.

And if you cannot come, then let the sea carry this: I loved you past language, past waking, past the last bright garden. I love you still, Mary, where all lost things are gathered—under the waves, inside the dream, in the mouth of every flower that opens and opens, though no one is there to see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an elegiac paragraph in a surreal, intimate style about mourning Mary and trying to preserve her through language and memory.
counterfactuals.output: Mary is gone, and still I find her everywhere: folded into the blue vein of evening, sleeping beneath the dust on the piano, breathing faintly inside the vowels of her name. I write her down to keep the dark from finishing its work, though each sentence is only a small glass jar lowered into the sea. Memory alters her tenderly—gives her moth wings, a dress sewn from rain, a voice that opens the locked rooms of winter—and I let it, because accuracy belongs to the living. What I want is her warmth beside me, the impossible weight of her hand; what I have are words, those pale animals, circling the place where she vanished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem in which the speaker repeatedly invokes the name “Mary,” wonders whether she is dead or asleep, and offers her pears, hyacinths, and other dreamlike images.
counterfactuals.output: Mary, are you dead, or only asleep beneath the blue weight of morning? I have brought pears in a silver bowl, each one holding a small green dusk. Mary, open your hands. The hyacinths have filled the room with their purple bells, though no wind enters and no one has rung them. I have set a glass of rain beside your bed, a feather from the moon, three buttons lost by angels. Mary, are you asleep, or has death taught you this perfect stillness? Outside, the orchard drifts through the fog like a ship whose sailors have forgotten the sea. A white horse kneels among the fallen fruit. The clocks are breathing backward. Mary, if you wake, I will cut the ripest pear and give you the half with the seeds. If you are dead, I will plant the seeds beneath your window, and every spring the branches will lean inward, bearing lanterns, bearing yellow birds, bearing the soft, impossible faces of those who dream they are alive. Mary, Mary, the hyacinths bow toward you. Tell me which world you are in, and whether there is room there for my voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental lament about absence, using lush antique imagery, sensual details, repetition, ampersands, and the idea that a beloved person survives only as a word.
counterfactuals.output:
### Reliquary for a Name

I opened the cedar chest & found  
no body—only linen,  
only the pale exhalation of lavender,  
only one black hair  
threaded through the teeth of an ivory comb.

You were gone & gone & gone,  
yet the mirrors kept your weather:  
a little rain of breath upon the glass,  
a gold dusk where your shoulders  
once undressed.

O vanished one,  
the figs split open on their silver plate,  
purple & honeyed, obscene with summer;  
the wine darkened in its Venetian cup;  
the candles leaned into their own warm ruin—

but you did not return.

I said your name.

The tapestries stirred:  
stags fled forever through embroidered forests,  
queens lifted their pearl-heavy throats,  
a falcon dreamed beneath its hood.

I said your name again.

Name, name—  
small bronze key with no lock,  
moth in the mouth,  
coin laid upon the tongue of the dead.

Once, your hands smelled of quince & smoke.  
Once, your lips were red as sealing wax.  
Once, beneath the damask canopy,  
you made of my body a chapel  
& entered without prayer.

Now the bed is a province of frost.  
Now the pillows keep no hollow.  
Now my skin remembers  
what the world denies.

& where are you?

Not in the garden, where the roses  
rot magnificently in their bowls.  
Not in the corridor, where marble saints  
hold their blank fingers to blank wounds.  
Not in the gramophone’s brass flower,  
though it opens & opens  
to pour out the old aria.

Only the word remains.

Your name on paper.  
Your name under glass.  
Your name, a pressed violet  
gone almost colorless.  
Your name in my mouth  
until my mouth is no longer a mouth  
but a crypt of syllables.

I polish the word with my tongue.  
I warm it between my breasts.  
I carry it through each room  
like a lamp whose oil is sorrow.

Beloved, beloved—

you survive as a word,  
& the word survives by wounding me.

At midnight I unfasten its letters  
one by one:  
the first like a clasp of jet,  
the second like a little bone,  
the third like a door  
opening onto no one.

No one & no one & no one.

Still, I gather the letters.  
Still, I string them on silk.  
Still, I wear them at my throat—

your absence, jeweled;  
your silence, perfumed;  
your name, the last warm thing

touching me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a haunting, stream-of-consciousness monologue to Mary about loss, mirrors, pillows, violets, sea foam, and the speaker’s inability to stop composing her.
counterfactuals.output:
Mary, I keep finding you where you cannot be—in the mirror after the candle gutters, in the hollow of the pillow where no head has rested since winter, in the bruised little violets pushing through the garden as if the earth were trying to remember the color of your eyes and getting it wrong, always wrong.

I tell the mirror you are gone. It gives you back to me in fragments: your shoulder in my shoulder, your mouth moving beneath mine, your pale face hovering just behind the glass. When I turn, there is only the room, holding its breath. When I turn back, you have vanished again, and I am left with my own reflection wearing the expression of someone who has heard her name called from underwater.

Mary.

Even saying it is a kind of drowning.

At night I press my face into your pillow. It has forgotten you more quickly than I have. The linen smells of dust, rain, the faint mineral cold of an unopened grave. I search its folds for one hair, one salt of you, one small proof that you once lay beside me and dreamed without knowing I was awake, listening to your breath rise and fall like the sea beyond the cliffs.

The sea keeps making you. It gathers itself, breaks, and there you are in the foam—white wrists, white throat, the hem of your dress dissolving among the stones. Then the water draws you backward by the ankles, and I run after you, though every wave erases the path of the last. Perhaps loss is only this: the world endlessly composing a body and refusing to let it remain.

I bring violets to the shore. Foolish, I know. They darken in my fist like little wounds. I scatter them on the water and watch each one become an eye, closing.

Forgive me, Mary. I cannot stop composing you.

I compose you from mirrors and pillows, from sea foam caught in black weeds, from the blue hush beneath a violet’s tongue. I give you hands because I miss their weight. I give you a voice because silence has learned yours too well. I give you a heartbeat, then another, then another—but each time I finish, you look at me with that terrible gentleness and die inside the sentence.

Still I begin again.

Mary at the window. Mary asleep. Mary laughing with rain in her hair. Mary turning toward me before the door closes. Mary not yet lost. Mary never born. Mary everywhere, Mary nowhere, Mary written until the ink thins to seawater and the page shines like a mirror—

and there, behind me,

you almost breathe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
